{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"When an update moves a privacy setting from one menu to another, the change can feel larger than a rearranged screen. A familiar control suddenly has a new address, and its label may change as well (even when the underlying choice remains available). That moment reveals why software settings should remain legible after updates.

Legibility means that a person can recognize what a setting governs, locate it, and understand the consequence of changing it. The standard does not require an interface to stay frozen. Software can gain features, combine menus, or revise its design. But those changes should preserve a clear path from a person’s intention to the control that carries it.

A moved setting creates a practical problem: memory becomes unreliable. Someone who once found a control quickly must search again, while a renamed control adds a second layer of uncertainty (the old term no longer points cleanly to the new one). The difficulty is modest in a single moment, but repeated updates turn ordinary maintenance into a maze.

Clear labels and stable explanations reduce that burden. If a setting changes location, its description can identify the function plainly and indicate the new place (for example, beneath a different heading). If its name changes, the interface can preserve familiar language alongside the new term, at least long enough for the transition to be understood.

This matters because settings are part of the user’s control over software. An update may improve the product, but it’s still a failure of communication when a meaningful choice becomes hard to recognize. The setting doesn’t need to look identical forever; it needs to remain findable and intelligible. A system can change its surface without hiding its workings.

We should expect updates to explain their changes in the same clear language the settings themselves use. A short notice, a preserved description, or a visible path to the revised control can keep a rearrangement from becoming confusion. Software should evolve, but it can’t make control depend on memory of an older interface. Keep the settings legible, and keep the person’s choice within reach.","omitted":[{"habit":"opponents-allies-sources / o11: attributed opposing positions tested against sources","why":"The request supplies no real opposing position or source material, and inventing either would violate the factual constraint."}],"refused":""}
